<reason>Both sides were skilled, but PRO built the cleaner decision path. CON's strongest attack was that PRO treated administrative data as decisive when favourable and confounded when not; PRO answered this squarely and principledly with a stated, symmetric criterion (does the design measure the family form or family disruption — continuous same-sex households versus who shares an address on census night), and explicitly offered to discount registry work that failed the same test. CON never engaged that criterion in Rebuttal 2, pivoting instead to "the decisive study was never run," which left CON's own headline evidence (the Canadian graduation finding) exposed to exactly the confound CON had accused PRO of ignoring. PRO also kept the burden symmetric — refusing placement on the basis of a parent's sex is itself a policy needing evidence — and showed that CON's bar is met by exactly one family form, which CON conceded in A4.1, making the standard look like a ratified presumption rather than an evidentiary test. On stability, PRO's input-versus-outcome distinction (we can look at the children directly rather than argue about predicted inputs) blunted CON's best mechanism play, forcing CON into a global scepticism about all outcome measurement that PRO named memorably as "a verdict wearing a lab coat." CON did land real hits: the variance/height analogy went unanswered, the "equalize now on evidence you hope will exist later" jab on legal recognition stung, and the triage-versus-statute distinction held well enough to blunt the foster-child dilemma. But CON's route ultimately rests on absence of evidence plus a predicted mechanism, and PRO showed the asymmetry that the alternative policy has no evidence either. PRO's two clipped over-length turns are a genuine execution cost against a clean CON, which narrows the margin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1 in Rebuttal 2 (B4.1–B4.2), answering CON's consistency charge with a stated, applies-both-ways design criterion based on exposure measurement rather than data type — which both defused CON's sharpest attack and turned CON's own census-based graduation finding into the confound CON had accused PRO of. CON's failure to engage that criterion in its next speech was the decisive gap.</best_rebuttal>
